exercises.prompt: Implement a class Counter that tracks an integer count. Its constructor takes an optional start value that defaults to 0. It has three methods: inc() adds 1 to the count, dec() subtracts 1, and value() returns the current count. A new Counter() starts at 0, and after two inc() calls value() is 2. Separate Counter instances hold independent counts.

tests.setup: const c = new Counter()

const c = new Counter()
c.inc()
c.inc()
c.inc()

const c = new Counter()
c.inc()
c.dec()
c.dec()

hints: Store the count on the instance as this.count in the constructor, then have each method read or change it.
inc() and dec() adjust this.count with ++ and --, while value() returns it.
Set this.count = start in the constructor and use this.count++, this.count--, and return this.count — because each new Counter() gets its own this.count, incrementing a stays invisible to b.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class Stack — a last-in, first-out collection. Its constructor takes no arguments and starts empty. push(x) adds x on top; pop() removes and returns the top element; peek() returns the top element WITHOUT removing it; size() returns how many elements are stored. After push(1) then push(2), pop() returns 2. On a new empty stack size() is 0.

tests.setup: const s = new Stack()

const s = new Stack()
s.push(1)
s.push(2)
s.push(3)

const s = new Stack()
s.push('a')
s.push('b')
s.peek()

hints: Back the stack with a plain array on the instance — this.items = [] in the constructor — and let the array's own methods do the work.
Array push and pop already give last-in-first-out; peek reads the last element without removing it, and size is the array's length.
return this.items.pop() for pop and this.items[this.items.length - 1] for peek — peek must not call pop, or the size-after-peek test would drop to 1 instead of staying at 2.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class BankAccount. Its constructor takes an optional starting balance that defaults to 0. deposit(amount) adds amount to the balance; withdraw(amount) subtracts amount but throws a RangeError when amount is greater than the current balance (an overdraft); balance() returns the current balance. Withdrawing the exact balance is allowed and leaves 0. Separate accounts are independent.

tests.setup:
const a = new BankAccount(100)
a.deposit(50)

const a = new BankAccount(30)
a.withdraw(30)
const a = new BankAccount(50)
const a = new BankAccount(0)

hints: Keep the balance on the instance (this.bal), set from the constructor's start argument, and have each method read or adjust it.
In withdraw, guard first — if (amount > this.bal) throw new RangeError(...) — and only subtract when the funds are there; that throwing call is what the raises tests exercise.

Use if (amount > this.bal) throw new RangeError('insufficient funds') before this.bal -= amount — the guard is > (not >=), so withdrawing exactly the balance succeeds and leaves 0, while over-withdrawing throws.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class Rectangle. Its constructor takes a width and a height and stores them. area() returns width × height, and perimeter() returns 2 × (width + height). For a Rectangle(3, 4), area() is 12 and perimeter() is 14. Two rectangles with different dimensions are independent.

tests.setup: const r = new Rectangle(3, 4)
const r = new Rectangle(3, 4)
const r = new Rectangle(5, 5)
const r = new Rectangle(10, 2)
const r = new Rectangle(7, 1)

const a = new Rectangle(2, 3)
const b = new Rectangle(4, 5)

hints: Save both dimensions in the constructor as this.width and this.height so every method can use them.
area() multiplies the two; perimeter() adds them and doubles the result.

return this.width * this.height for area and 2 * (this.width + this.height) for perimeter — keeping the two formulas distinct matters, since a Rectangle(3, 4) must give 12 and 14, not the same number.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class Queue — a first-in, first-out collection. Its constructor takes no arguments and starts empty. enqueue(x) adds x to the back; dequeue() removes and returns the front (oldest) element; size() returns how many elements are stored; isEmpty() returns true when the queue has no elements and false otherwise. After enqueue(1) then enqueue(2), dequeue() returns 1 — the first one in.

tests.setup:
const q = new Queue()
q.enqueue('a')
q.enqueue('b')
q.enqueue('c')

const q = new Queue()
q.enqueue(1)
q.enqueue(2)
q.dequeue()
const q = new Queue()

const q = new Queue()
q.enqueue(1)

const q = new Queue()
q.enqueue(1)
q.enqueue(2)
q.dequeue()
q.dequeue()

hints: Back the queue with an array on the instance; the difference from a stack is which end you remove from.
enqueue adds to the back with push; dequeue removes from the FRONT with shift, giving first-in-first-out; isEmpty checks whether the length is 0.
return this.items.shift() for dequeue — shift removes the oldest element, so the first test returns 1; using pop instead would return 2 and turn the queue into a stack.
